title: Audi lodge 'intention to appeal' over Tsunoda decision
excerpt:
Audi have notified the FIA of their "intention to appeal" after Yuki Tsunoda avoided any penalty for a potential starting infraction at the Italian Grand Prix.

Following Charles Leclerc's crash on the second lap of Sunday's 53-lap race at Monza, the red flag was deployed to repair barrier damage before a standing restart took place.

However, drivers were sent round for a further formation lap after Tsunoda, making his second appearance of the season for Racing Bulls, made a late change of direction into the correct grid box when he realised he was heading for the wrong grid position.

Once the race resumed, Tsunoda eventually finished in 10th to claim the final point on offer, with the Japanese driver not penalised due to several factors, according to the stewards.

"Car 22 approached the grid initially heading for the left hand side of the grid, then realising he was headed for the wrong grid position, the driver changed direction and positioned his car in the correct grid box and in the correct position within the grid box," read the stewards' document on the incident.

"This was verified by the stewards with video from multiple camera angles. The Race Director, in evidence, stated that it was his call, based on the behaviour of the car on the approach to the grid box, to commence an extra formation lap. He stated he was not comfortable starting the race with the car in that position."

The document went on to say that "at no time was the team advised that Race Control considered Car 22 to be the cause of the extra formation lap", and so couldn't advise Tsunoda to start from the pit lane as per Article B5.9.4 of the F1 2026 sporting regulations.

The stewards ultimately concluded that "the extra formation lap resulted from the Race Director’s assessment of the situation, rather than being directly caused by the driver of Car 22."

Audi driver Gabriel Bortoleto finished P11, just missing out on points and prompting the team to inform the FIA of its intention to appeal.

A statement from Audi read: "Following the Italian Grand Prix, we raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4, which requires a driver who causes an extra formation lap to enter the pit lane and resume the race from there.

"The stewards issued a decision of No Further Action, and we have notified our intention to appeal. As the matter is now subject to the FIA appeal process, we will not comment further at this stage."

title: Could Antonelli have won the Italian GP without the VSC?
excerpt:
Lining up 19th on the grid of his home Italian Grand Prix, Kimi Antonelli must have been cursing the Mercedes algorithms.

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said it was the algorithm that dictated Antonelli take a back-of-grid engine penalty at his home race because the computers “don’t take [drivers’] nationality into consideration”.

Those same systems told him he had no chance of winning the race. A top-five finish was his likely result, and even after making his monumental comeback to lead the race on Lap 18, his tyre strategy should have limited him to second place at best.

title: What the teams said – Race day in Italy
excerpt:
Mercedes

Kimi Antonelli became the first Italian to win at Monza since 1966, which considering he started from 19th on the grid was an incredible result and arguably his best victory to date. He had an electric first lap, and found himself 12th when the red flags came out. Another brilliant first lap at the second start saw him eighth, and from there he quickly climbed up to run second behind his team mate.

George Russell had grabbed the lead from Gasly on Lap 2, and then jostled with Verstappen up front. He fought with Antonelli across a number of laps, the lead swapping before the team seemed to call off the fight with Verstappen’s threatening from third.

Then came the decisive moment – Antonelli on worn mediums pitting under a VSC, Russell on the hards staying out. On fresh tyres, Antonelli scythed his way back to his team mate, and took the lead and ultimately a famous win, via one hairy moment through the gravel.

Kimi Antonelli, 1st

"This is a day that I will remember forever! It is for sure the most special win of my career so far. It is the best podium of the season and to see the full pit straight packed with people cheering and showing their support was a dream. The team did an incredible job today; they gave us an amazing car, and I can't say thank you enough to everyone that has supported me and helped get me to this point.

"Even starting P19, I believed that this might be possible. On the first start, I made up a lot of positions and then realised we would get another good chance to gain positions after the red flag. That gave us a good chance, and I felt that I had the speed to fight for the win. We obviously gave up some positions under the Virtual Safety Car, but we had the pace on the Medium tyre to come back through and take the victory."

George Russell, 2nd

"It's frustrating to be so close to victory and not to achieve it but that is racing sometimes. Despite that, it is a brilliant result for the team, and I want to say massive congratulations to Kimi on winning his home race. There are many positives both I and the team will take away from this weekend. We showed great pace all weekend and fought hard throughout.

"The Virtual Safety Car was definitely a moment where the race changed. At the time, no one could have known what the right call was. The team chose to split strategy between the two cars and that was the best decision we could have made. We will never know how the race might have unfolded otherwise but Kimi did an amazing job. We raced each other hard but always with respect, and it was good fun fighting wheel-to-wheel for the win."

Toto Wolff, Head of Mercedes-Benz Motorsport

"That was a phenomenal race by the team and both drivers. To take a 1-2 in Monza is a special feeling and victory will obviously be particularly sweet for Kimi at his home race. Both Kimi and George drove brilliantly and were comfortably faster than the rest of the field. Even though they were battling at moments, they kept it clean and brought home a big points haul which is incredibly valuable at this stage in the championship.

"Kimi's drive was methodical from the very start. He kept his head down, took no risks on both starts and just one-by-one began picking off the cars ahead of him. We didn't think his first set of Medium tyres would go to the end, so the Virtual Safety Car gave him a cheaper stop; his pace was superb to make the strategy work. For George, he ran the conventional strategy but was suffering with some vibrations on his front tyres in the closing stages. That limited his pace slightly, but he still drove strongly throughout to take P2."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"Today was a well-executed race by the whole team and overall, a strong weekend throughout. Even with Kimi starting near the back, we were confident that he could move forward and potentially fight for the podium. We had done a lot of work to optimise our race pace on Friday and that showed in the Grand Prix. Both Kimi and George were significantly faster than their competitors and that was brilliant to see.

"The decision to either pit or stay out under the Virtual Safety Car was a close one. Ultimately, we decided to split strategies across cars to give ourselves the best chance of victory. Pitting Kimi was different to what most of the top 10 did but enabled us to cover threats from the opposition. At that point, the one-stop looked like the slightly stronger strategy, but Kimi's pace really made the two-stop work. He carved past cars we thought he may struggle to pass; both Kimi and George were incredibly quick but once Kimi had caught, the tyre age offset meant he was able to pass quickly.

"Our pace this weekend has been encouraging. We know we are out of sync with our rivals in terms of updates so to take a 1-2 and increase our lead in the championships is pleasing. We know that Monza is an outlier as a track though and we cannot expect this form to continue into Madrid next week. That will be a much tougher fight; we will once again focus on executing a clean weekend, maximising the package we have and bringing home good points."

title: Why Gasly won’t be ‘disappointed’ with P7 from pole for Alpine
excerpt:
Usually a Formula 1 driver who starts from pole position and tumbles down to seventh won’t be too happy with such an outcome, but that wasn’t the case for Pierre Gasly in Monza.

As much as Gasly dared to dream that circumstances might allow him at least make it to the podium, the Frenchman and his Alpine team knew that the numbers didn’t add up.

The A526 was superb over one lap on Saturday. However, it was always going to struggle to hold its own against Mercedes, Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari over a race distance.

The retirement of Charles Leclerc and a difficult race for Liam Lawson opened up a couple of spots among the top eight places, and that allowed the Frenchman to take a respectable P7, well clear of the rest of the usual midfield contenders.

The 2020 Italian Grand Prix winner also crossed the line on the tail of a Ferrari and only 27.3 seconds behind winner Kimi Antonelli.

“I mean, the part of me that is realistic is very satisfied,” said Gasly. “Basically, starting on pole, you must have a side of you which thinks, ‘Okay, what can happen over 53 laps, this and that?’ But I've got to be honest, before the race, we knew that with the pace in the race it would be extremely difficult to stay up there and fight with the top guys.

“I'm very happy with the two starts – we took two great starts, managed to keep the lead on the first one, great on the second, battled slightly, stayed in the right train for the first 10 laps, which was really good. And we battled with Lando Norris, who won the last two races.

“So from where we come from, it's very positive and finished three seconds behind Lewis, who has been fighting for podium this year, so I'm not going to be disappointed with that.

“Obviously, the end result is P7, and you'll wish you can get slightly more out of it. But I think overall we've just got to try to take all the positives from the weekend, because there were many and try to build from that.”

Antonelli's Italian GP victory a 'dream coming true

“It's been a lot going on, for sure,” he said. “The last 24 hours has been extremely fun and extremely enjoyable with all the energy, the motivation in the garage, the reaction of the whole team. I'm sure it's going to bring a huge boost to all of us.

“And as I say, from where we came last year to today, I was looking at the cars ahead, they were a couple seconds in front of us. We finished 18 seconds ahead of Arvid, so the gap with the cars in front was smaller than the gap with the car behind. So that's what we've got to build on, and hopefully we can repeat this type of performance more often.”

The good news is that Gasly can see Alpine making progress in all areas.

“I’m very happy with the steps I'm seeing everywhere, in terms of car performance, in terms of executions, in terms of how we approach the weekend,” he said. “We're raising the bar all the time. And again, a few things we know on race day which we're missing with the car, like help with the tyres, et cetera. So we still have stuff to learn and do better. But overall, I think we're very well aware, and we are heading in the right direction.

“For the team, I think the last pole was in 2009. Imagine some guys that have been working there for years and never experienced it! And I'm sure going back to Enstone is going to be quite special. And again, that should be the target, try to repeat it and get a bit better on Sunday, and try to be in that mix in front of us.”

Meanwhile it was a race of frustration for Gasly’s team mate Franco Colapinto. On the one hand he had a great initial start, getting up to fourth prior to the red flag. He then gained another spot by passing Max Verstappen at the restart to briefly take third.

However, he then made a mistake and ran through the gravel, which dropped him to P15. After that it was a hard slog back to P9 and a couple of precious points.

"I just lost the car completely in Turn 5, [Turn] 6, a bit out of nowhere,” the Argentinian said. “You feel so strong, and suddenly fighting with the top teams, you get very motivated very quickly, and a mistake like that throws it all away. Just frustrated. I don't really understand yet what happened. I lost the car very aggressively, I went very fast through the gravel. I had a lot of damage.”

This was the first time that Colapinto had a chance to go wheel-to-wheel with the biggest names in the sport: “That's why I think it's so frustrating. P7 to P3, it's very good. I got four of the top teams' cars, and that's why it hurts so much to throw it away. Being up there with them, you don't realise that it's not really your fight.

“You want to keep going and taking risks, and maybe it didn't make sense. I have just to learn from it and try to improve for the next time I get a chance for this.”

title: Lindblad pleased with ‘damage limitation’ for Racing Bulls
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad described his and stand-in team mate Yuki Tsunoda’s double points finish at the Italian Grand Prix as “damage limitation” for Racing Bulls after Alpine’s eye-catching Qualifying display.

Racing Bulls and Alpine are both pushing to claim fifth in the Teams’ Championship and earn the ‘best of the rest’ title this season – behind front-runners Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull.

Alpine looked set to make major moves at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza when Pierre Gasly charged his way to a shock pole position, with Lindblad the lead Racing Bulls at the tail-end of the top 10 and Tsunoda falling at the Q1 hurdle.

However, the situation changed on Sunday when Gasly fell away from the leading group and ultimately crossed the line in seventh, ahead of Lindblad, the other Alpine of Franco Colapinto and Tsunoda, who recovered well from the back.

The result means Racing Bulls remain P5 in the championship on 75 points, with Alpine on 62, and their next nearest rivals Haas on 21.

Speaking after the race, Lindblad said: “I think on a weekend where Alpine have brought something special on the straights, to be able to split them is very good.

“It’s a very small loss to them when in reality Pierre was starting on pole and I was starting P10, so to finish right behind him is good. I think it’s damage limitation for us, so we can be happy as a team.”

With Lindblad scoring points in seven of the last eight Grands Prix, he added: “I think obviously for me it’s a confidence booster, but also it’s credit to the team. We do have a strong car, it’s a robust car, it’s good on every circuit.

“Even today Alpine were much faster than us on the straights, but on the corners we were the same if not quicker. It was the same yesterday in Qualifying.

“In most tracks it’s corners that are the more important one. That gives us confidence for the upcoming rounds that we’ll still have the upper hand.”

Tsunoda finished 13 seconds behind Lindblad as he recovered from a tricky Qualifying session – and avoided a penalty for a potential start procedure infringement that the stewards looked into.

“I don’t have to talk about that, I guess?” Tsunoda smiled afterwards, having missed his grid slot at the race restart. “It’s been a bit of months that I was not racing. Some bit of confusion there. A very, very bad excuse!

“But it was a good race. A massive thanks to the team. Not bad, I think, having points after a bit of a break after Abu Dhabi [in 2025], so I’ll take it.

“It was really frustrating [to be out in Q1], because the pace was there, but at the same time, I’m happy that I brought these points back to the team now, especially when we’re fighting hard against Alpine.”

title: All the key moments from the 2026 Italian Grand Prix
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix delivered a thrilling afternoon of racing and an incredible comeback from Kimi Antonelli, who won his home race for the first time from 19th on the grid.

It was not such a positive outing in front of the Tifosi for Ferrari, however, with the Scuderia’s struggles proving to be one of several fascinating talking points that emerged from the event.

Here are all the key moments from the 2026 Italian Grand Prix…

Antonelli’s inspired home win (and Russell’s defeat)

As statement performances go, Kimi Antonelli’s drive to victory at Monza was an incredibly special one.

Heading into the weekend, all the talk on the Italian’s side of the garage was about damage limitation – sweeping power unit changes aboard his Mercedes leading to a hefty 30-place grid penalty.

However, Antonelli had other ideas, blending rapid raw pace and smart overtakes from the outset of Sunday’s race to charge through the field and put himself on the tail of team mate George Russell before the halfway mark.

He was 12th after just a couple of tours when Race Control threw a red flag for Charles Leclerc’s heavy crash, worked his way into the points shortly after the restart, and made an initial move on Russell for the lead on Lap 18.

A mid-race Virtual Safety Car played its part in the intra-team battle, with Antonelli pitting for fresh medium tyres and Russell staying out on used hards, but there was no denying the home racer’s underlying pace. Mercedes boss Toto Wolff even claimed afterwards that “nothing would have stopped him” from taking the chequered flag first.

The result means Antonelli now sits 66 points clear of Russell in the championship standings, only nine points shy of a three-win cushion. It will take some response from the Briton in the coming races to stop the youngster from storming to the 2026 crown…

Wolff heaps praise on Antonelli for 'amazing' Monza charge

A ‘devastating’ home race for Ferrari after Lap 1 drama

While Antonelli enjoyed a dream outing in his local Grand Prix, Ferrari’s homecoming proved a much tougher affair.

The team arrived at Monza with high hopes, with Lewis Hamilton admitting on Thursday that he “strongly believed” in the squad’s victory chances at an event where they would be bringing an engine upgrade, while Charles Leclerc stated that he would aim for a “very special weekend”.

This goal hit a snag on Saturday when both drivers were left feeling that the team’s strategy could have been executed more effectively in Qualifying, the session having left the pair in fourth and fifth – which became third and fourth on the grid following a penalty for Oscar Piastri ahead.

When Sunday’s Grand Prix got underway, third-placed Leclerc and Hamilton went wheel-to-wheel into the second corner and Hamilton subsequently ran wide into the gravel, dropping him down the order. “Charles pushed me off!” the seven-time World Champion radioed in.

One lap later, Leclerc’s charge came to an early end when he lost control of his SF-26 and crashed into the barriers, the Monegasque explaining later that he “had to go back off and on throttle” during the first tour and would have to “look into” what happened.

Hamilton, meanwhile, went on to cross the line in only sixth place. The Briton labelled his race as “a bit devastating” and “tough to swallow”, adding of his early incident with Leclerc: “I ended up P10 or something. There's not really much to say. We'll take it offline.”

Gasly delivers the shock of the season with pole

While the advantage of a slipstream in Qualifying meant a surprise result was always possible, no one expected Pierre Gasly and Alpine to snatch an incredible pole position at Monza on Saturday afternoon.

But Gasly's maiden Formula 1 pole position – at a venue where he scored his first and so far only victory six years ago – was no fluke. The Frenchman utilised the Mercedes power unit to go fastest in both Q1 and, when it mattered most, in Q3 to claim arguably the shock of the season.

“I’m so happy. It’s been nine years [in F1] trying to chase and get the opportunity to take pole position," said Gasly after his Qualifying heroics. "I won my first race in Monza, and to get my first pole position on this track… I think is something special around here.”

The prospect of holding out against the top teams over 53 laps in Sunday's race was always going to be a step too far, and so it proved, despite leading the opening lap and circulating amongst the leading runners for a time.

Ultimately, Gasly eventually slipped down to seventh in the final classification, 27 seconds adrift of race winner Antonelli but well clear of the chasing pack.

Team mate Franco Colapinto also reached the points in P9, having run as high as third at the restart. Going off the track at Lesmo 1 dropped him down the order, before a spirited fightback meant he passed Yuki Tsunoda's Racing Bulls in the closing laps.

Colapinto fell short of reaching the second Racing Bulls machine of Arvid Lindblad in P8, but the result means Alpine have closed the gap to the Red Bull sister outfit in their battle for P5 in the teams' standings, with the margin now sitting at 13 points.

The F1 drivers who waited longest for a first pole position

Lightning McQueen stars in bumper pre-race show

The Tifosi might not have been thrilled by Ferrari’s final result, but they were certainly given a show before Sunday’s action kicked off, including a special appearance by one of the undisputed greats of racing – Lightning McQueen.

To celebrate the 20-year anniversary of the release of Disney and Pixar’s Cars, McQueen lined up alongside the Safety Car, which sported a Cars-themed livery of its own, before completing an honorary lap ahead of the race.

It marked another chapter in the collaboration between Disney and F1, and it wasn’t just the fans who revelled in McQueen’s run – Liam Lawson, who has shared his love of the film on multiple occasions, paid a visit to him earlier in the weekend and was presented with his very own Piston Cup.

Grid Gigs also returned to add to the pre-race spectacle, with Italian singer Laura Pausini performing an energetic set prior to the drivers’ arrival on the grid.

Duerksen and Lacorte grab wins in Monza as F2 and F3 delight the crowds

Joshua Duerksen won the F2 Feature Race in fine style for Invicta Racing, leading home his team mate Rafael Camara with Campos Racing’s Noel Leon completing the rostrum.

Duerksen also won the Sprint, meaning he has a record-equalling eight wins in F2, the Paraguayan driver having a stunning weekend at Monza. The results lift him to eighth in the championship, with Camara’s podium helping to close the gap to leader Nikola Tsolov.

Tsolov leads by 11 points, with racing set to resume in Madrid next weekend.

In F3, Nicola Lacorte grabbed his maiden victory for DAMS Lucas Oil. It was an emotional win for the Italian on home soil, the 19-year-old coming through from third on the grid to grab his team’s first F3 victory.

MP Motorsport’s Tuukka Taponen and Taito Kato (ART Grand Prix) rounded out the podium, as championship contender Freddie Slater retired with what appeared a mechanical issue. His rival Ugo Ugochukwu fought his way to eighth from the back of the field, to narrow the deficit between the two to just 15 points.

One round remains, with the title set to be decided in Madrid next weekend.

title: Norris and Piastri reflect on 'good battle' in Italy
excerpt:
Lando Norris believes his late tussle with McLaren team mate Oscar Piastri in the Italian Grand Prix was “a good battle” which was “fair”, despite initially complaining over the radio.

Despite entering the weekend at Monza having taken two consecutive wins, reigning World Champion Norris was only able to start P8 for Sunday’s 53-lap race.

The Briton was able to make steady progress though, and was challenging Piastri for P4, sealing the position on the final lap into the Ascari Chicane, but only after an earlier moment where Norris took to the grass.

“No, it was okay," said Norris when reflecting on the incident on the exit of Curva Grande and heading into the second chicane.

“I still need to review things, but I think it's just a perception of when you're in the car, when someone's kind of opening the gap a bit and then kind of go straight, you get that perception when you're going at 200mph. So that's all.

“But I think what he did was fair. It's just when you're in the moment and you're half on the grass, you realise how quickly things can end pretty badly – just in the heat of the moment. But from that side it was fine, and was a good battle. So yeah, a good result from a tough race.”

Piastri started P6 after being handed a three-place grid drop for blocking Liam Lawson in Qualifying, and the Australian battled Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari for much of the race.

Having been unable to keep pace with Max Verstappen on a fresh set of tyres ahead, Piastri ultimately fell into the clutches of Norris, but also believed their battle to be fair.

"It was a tough battle for sure. I think we both seemed pretty even, especially in the last few laps, so it was definitely challenging to know when to use your battery, when not to," he said.

“I think that we saw a good battle. From my point of view, I thought it was good racing – exciting, that's for sure, and ultimately I think that was the best result we could have got as a team, so I'm pretty happy with it.”

Leclerc explains Monza crash as he reacts to ‘way too close’ Hamilton

Despite having the same power unit as Mercedes, which claimed a 1-2 with Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, McLaren were unable to extract the same performance.

The progress of Piastri and Norris wasn't helped by losing the tow to the Mercedes drivers and Verstappen ahead in the middle phase of the race, leaving them out of the slipstream and adrift.

“We needed someone to kind of pull us along, and then we could compete, because then we're more on a level playing field compared to them," said Norris.

"I think on a day like today, it was almost a good thing to not be ahead for too often, because generally you would always go backwards.

“But then when you were behind, you always felt like you could go forwards. So it was always a tough position to be in. Sometimes you just had to be a little bit patient, and kind of for me, that worked on the final two laps. I think P4 was the best we could achieve, and P4 and P5 for us as a team is also good.”

title: Ferrari's Italian GP result 'devastating' – Hamilton
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton admits that finishing only sixth in the Italian Grand Prix is a "tough one to swallow", as Ferrari endured a difficult home race.

The Tifosi had high hopes ahead of Sunday's 53-lap race at Monza, with Hamilton starting fourth and directly behind Ferrari team mate, Charles Leclerc.

But things began to unravel as early as the first corner, with Hamilton moving up the inside of Leclerc, only to find himself in the gravel on the exit of Turn 2 which dropped the seven-time World Champion to the fringes of the top 10.

"Well I ended up P10 or something. There's not really much to say. We'll take it offline," said Hamilton when asked what impact the moment had on his race.

Leclerc's race came to an end at the final corner on Lap 2, the Monegasque driver suffering an over correction before hitting the barrier hard which brought out a red flag.

On the Hamilton incident, Leclerc said: "With Lewis it was a way too close into Turn 1 and unfortunately in Turn 2 – I don't know if we had contact or whatsoever.

"I was quite a lot on the inside curve and tried to make the corner, which I didn't do it tight enough, and then I obviously only saw in the mirrors what happened which is never what you want between between two cars of the same team."

At the restart, Hamilton started on the medium tyre and battled Oscar Piastri's McLaren for P4 initially, but unlike other drivers who were running on the medium-walled Pirelli tyre, he did not pit under a mid-race Virtual Safety Car.

It meant Hamilton lost further positions to the recovering Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen, as well as Lando Norris before reaching the chequered flag a distant sixth.

"A bit devastating. Tough one to swallow. Lost a lot of points and ultimately couldn't keep a Mercedes engine behind. They were just out and out quicker," said Hamilton.

"I think we probably chose the wrong tyre. Whether that really would have made much difference, maybe we would have been able to hold onto them a bit longer but they just kept flying past us. They were just quicker today."

title: Verstappen happy with Monza P3 despite issue that ‘cost a lot’
excerpt:
Max Verstappen was pleased to come away from the Italian Grand Prix with a podium finish in P3, having conceded after the race that a lack of deployment in comparison to other cars “cost us a lot”.

Starting from fifth on the grid, Verstappen had climbed up to third in the opening laps – and when the event was restarted following a crash for Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, the Dutchman even moved up into the lead at one stage.

While he was eventually overtaken by the Mercedes cars of George Russell and Kimi Antonelli, there was another charge for Verstappen when he pitted for fresh tyres under a later Virtual Safety Car phase.

The four-time World Champion enjoyed a number of battles – admitting later that he “had to send it many times around the outside” – en route to a third place finish.

Speaking in more detail about the Grand Prix later on, Verstappen explained why he was particularly pleased with the result as he detailed what he had struggled with.

“I tried to battle but we were just too slow on the straight,” said Verstappen. “We just lacked the same deployment, and that basically cost us a lot because at one point it's not defendable anymore.

“Once of course I had Kimi and George in front of me, I could just hang into the Overtake Mode. We just lack a bit of deployment on tracks like this, but for us to be on the podium is a very good result.”

Quizzed on the overtakes he had made – and whether being able to fight was a positive to take from the weekend – Verstappen responded: “I mean, I had to.

“I was so slow on the straight that the only chance was just to try and brake late and try to get my positions back all the time, in the start, if we were battling, but it worked. So, of course, happy with that and happy to be on the podium.“

title: Red Bull set 'ultimate speed' target after Max Verstappen heroics
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has set the Austrian marque the target of finding "that ultimate speed", something he feels it is lacking despite Max Verstappen's heroic Monza podium.

The Dutchman started the Italian Grand Prix from fifth and quickly worked his way towards the front, overtaking Charles Leclerc and Pierre Gasly in rapid fashion.

Verstappen's early-race pace was impressive, with the four-time world champion even briefly taking the lead after passing George Russell.

However, the 28-year-old quickly fell back behind Russell and then Kimi Antonelli, who charged through the field to win from 19th on the grid.

A mid-race pit stop for fresh tyres dropped Verstappen to seventh, although he worked his way back through the field to claim an impressive third-place podium finish.

It was the best on offer for the Red Bull star, with Mercedes simply having a pace advantage that he could not compete with throughout the race.

Mekies was in awe of what Verstappen achieved and hopes that finding better car speed will improve the team's overall performance.

"It was a well-deserved podium for Max and the whole team," said Mekies. "It was an intense weekend, but the race showed that our pace was fairly strong.

"Mercedes was a bit too fast for us but we were strong enough to beat Ferrari and McLaren on merits. It was probably our best race pace in a few weeks and a step in the right direction.

"We won't be happy until we have that ultimate speed and we clearly still have some challenges to overcome, which may unlock more performance once we get to the bottom of them.

"Max has been incredible on track. He made several very spectacular overtakes and defensive manoeuvres and drove an aggressive strategy which led us to the podium."

title: Kimi Antonelli opens up on victory-chance belief after stunning recovery
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has opened up on whether he believed victory was possible in the Italian Grand Prix after his stunning recovery to win from 19th on home soil.

The championship leader started from the penultimate row of the grid following a power unit change, with the components having been outside of his legal pool.

Going into the race, the Italian had hopes of a podium, although his eyes quickly turned to a potential race win after climbing to 12th before a red flag on the third lap.

From the race restart, Antonelli made rapid progress towards the front, where he exchanged positions with George Russell on several occasions.

Antonelli ultimately dropped to sixth after pitting during a short Virtual Safety Car period, but, on fresher tyres, he breezed to the front to claim a famous win.

Asked what he thought was possible on the grid, Antonelli said: "I thought a podium was possible, but then obviously with the red flag I was already P12, and then I knew that I could have had a shot to it.

"But, of course, you know, then I found myself at the front and battling, but it was very difficult to break away, basically impossible. So I knew it would have been difficult.

"Then with the VSC we pitted and then we had to close the gap and, yeah, then in the end to bring it home, very happy with that."

Monza boasts arguably the most incredible podium celebrations of the season, which were further heightened by the fact that Antonelli was the first Italian winner of the Italian GP since 1966.

It was an emotional occasion for the youngster, who now leads the drivers' championship by 66 points over Russell.

Discussing the reaction from the fans while on the podium, Antonelli added: Yeah, I think this is the most special podium of the season.

"To see all the fans on the straight, it’s just incredible. And then, of course, you know, being at home, it adds that little bit of extra. And, yeah, super, super happy with that."

title: Charles Leclerc hits back at anti-teamwork Lewis Hamilton 'narrative'
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has hit back at a "narrative" that he and Lewis Hamilton are not working together following a disastrous Italian Grand Prix.

Discussions about the Ferrari pair not working together were brought up in Zandvoort before it all went horribly wrong at the first two corners in Monza.

Both Scuderia drivers started on the second row, with Hamilton opting for an aggressive move down the inside of Leclerc at the first corner.

This forced Leclerc to take a different line into Turn 2, which resulted in his seven-time world champion teammate being left with nowhere to go but the gravel on the exit of the corner.

Hamilton tumbled from fourth to 10th and immediately complained over the radio, only for Leclerc to crash out of the race at the end of the second lap and trigger a red flag.

Leclerc lost control of his SF-26 on the exit of Parabolica, resulting in barrier repairs being needed while his destroyed car also required retrieval.

However, what happened at the first corners came up after the race in the media pen, with Leclerc insisting that the talk of the duo not working together was false.

Asked about the narrative of himself and Hamilton not working together, the Monegasque told select media, including RacingNews365: "Yeah, I don't really know who is forcing that narrative that we are one against the other.

"I mean, honestly, Zandvoort, there were way too many talks already. Here, it's true, though, that we went too far.

"I think Lewis in Turn 1, then Turn 2, I tried to do the tightest corner possible, but that was just not enough. And doing it here is not good."

title: Franco Colapinto breaks down in tears after 'wasted' opportunity
excerpt:
A crestfallen Franco Colapinto could not conceal his emotions after an error at the restart of the Italian Grand Prix saw him tumble down the order from third on the road.

The Alpine driver, who started seventh at Monza, cleverly capitalised on the Charles Leclerc-induced red flag to get himself into fourth, dumping his remaining battery and passing Oscar Piastri before the race was stopped.

At the resumption, the Argentine driver briefly overtook Max Verstappen for third, behind team-mate Pierre Gasly, but made a costly mistake at the first Lesmo corner.

Running fourth at the time, Colapinto ran wide onto the gravel, falling to P15 as any chance of the Alpines working together fell by the wayside.

Speaking on TV after the 53-lap contest, the 23-year-old was distraught and could not hold back his tears, having thrown away a crucial chance.

"It could have been... a great race and a... major mistake," the Alpine driver told ESPN and DAZN cameras in Spanish after the race.

"So... I wasted a very important opportunity for the team and for myself."

Nonetheless, Colapinto put together an impressive recovery drive, getting his A526 back up to ninth by the chequered flag, just two places behind Gasly in seventh, but he seemingly could not escape the feeling it could have been so much more.

He added: "So, a bit sad, but... I need to learn from this and keep pushing."

title: Max Verstappen hails Red Bull response after pointed criticism
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has commended Red Bull for the recovery the Milton Keynes-based outfit engineered with his RB22 across the Italian Grand Prix weekend, describing it as a "strong turnaround" after a bruising period for the team.

The four-time F1 drivers' champion finished on the podium at Monza, a result that seemed improbable just 48 hours earlier when he cut a frustrated figure during Friday practice, complaining of balance issues and a lack of pace after missing FP1 entirely due to Ayumu Iwasa's mandatory rookie running and ending FP2 only ninth fastest.

The round at the Temple of Speed came off the back of Red Bull's recent nadir at Zandvoort, where the Dutchman qualified a lowly seventh and crashed out on the opening lap in damp conditions.

He was blunt in his assessment there, saying the RB22 was "not really to my liking" and that Red Bull lacked the pace to fight at the front.

His criticism sharpened further in the build-up to Monza, where he warned the weekend would be "really painful" given the energy deployment limitations of his car — amid the controversial new power unit regulations — at such a power-hungry circuit. The pessimism appeared justified on Friday.

Yet Red Bull found something overnight, as the team so often does, given it has become somewhat of a calling card. Verstappen qualified sixth, benefited from Oscar Piastri's grid penalty, and went on to secure a podium finish in third behind the dominant Mercedes pair of Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

Masked problems

Even so, Verstappen made clear the result masked significant struggles during the race itself, particularly against Mercedes-powered machinery on Monza's long straights.

"I had my issues in qualifying that, of course, were still there," Verstappen told media, including RacingNews365. "But also, I think it was quite clear during the race that we just can't keep up with the deployment of the Mercedes-powered cars, and that is, of course, on a track like Monza, very tough.

"Of course, with the overtake mode it looked quite promising, but as soon as I got in the lead, it was very hard to defend, and that has been a bit my problem throughout the whole race.

"Even when we had the VSC, we boxed, had better tyres, I'm overtaking cars, but as soon as they, you know, can hang in that overtake mode, it's just too powerful for us to actually really defend that, even on better tyres. So, it took me a while even to clear the McLarens."

Despite those frustrations, Verstappen acknowledged the broader significance of the result given how far Red Bull had fallen at Zandvoort, where his first-lap retirement and the team's lack of competitiveness prompted pointed criticism of the car's direction.

"But for us to be on the podium, I think after a very difficult weekend in Zandvoort, where the car was not really to my liking, yeah, we managed to have a strong turnaround from Friday to Saturday, and the car was definitely in a better window," he added.

"But we still have a few bits and areas that we know need to be better, plus the obvious deployment on the straights."

title: Lewis Hamilton concedes to crucial Ferrari setback: 'Far too late'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes it is “far too late” for Ferrari to start increasing its teamwork in pursuit of the 2026 title.

Hamilton came to blows with Charles Leclerc on the opening lap, feeling he was pushed wide on the exit of Turn 2 by his team-mate.

The seven-time champion ran through the gravel and emerged down the order, forcing him into a recovery drive for the rest of the race.

Ferrari lost further ground to Mercedes after the Silver Arrows ended the race with maximum points, while Hamilton crossed the line in sixth place.

With Hamilton being closer to Mercedes in the standings than Leclerc for some time, some suggested at recent events that Ferrari should throw its support behind the former in order to maximise its chance of success this year.

But with Kimi Antonelli stretching out his lead following another win, Hamilton asserted it is too late for such decisions.

“We just lost so much ground on points [on Sunday],” Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

“It’s far too late for those decisions to come. It’s many, many weeks too late.

“All I can do is turn up. I’ll get up tomorrow morning and give my best.”

Ferrari's day went from bad to worse as Leclerc's race ended shortly after his skirmish with Hamilton, when he lost control of his car and crashed at the final corner.

While Hamilton did not completely rule out his chances of a title this year, he conceded the 76-point gap to Antonelli will likely be very difficult to overcome.

“Ultimately, I feel massively gutted for the Tifosi, who showed up for us today,” he said.

“The guys back at the factory, who really are giving it everything. [On Saturday] we didn’t really execute that well, and the same today.

“It’s tough because I’m giving it everything I can, but sometimes it’s not enough. You need all the other stuff to come together.

“It’s never over until it’s over.

“[But] it’s an amount that, with the pace that they have, it’s a very difficult amount to close up.”

title: F1 team submits intention to appeal Italian GP decision
excerpt:
Audi F1 team has notified the FIA of its intention to appeal the decision not to punish Yuki Tsunoda for a starting infringement at the Italian Grand Prix.

When the field lined up to take the restart at Monza following the Charles Leclerc-induced red flag, the Racing Bulls driver was at a strange angle in his grid slot, having initially lined up on the wrong side of the grid, which caused the stewards to trigger an extra formation lap.

Article B5.9.4 stipulates that a driver who is the cause of an extra formation lap must subsequently enter the pit lane and resume the race from there, which the Japanese driver did not do.

He was investigated by the stewards after the Italian Grand Prix, but the decision was that no further action would be taken against him.

The reason for that outcome was that he was deemed to have been correctly within his grid slot, albeit at an unusual angle and that the race director decided to instigate a new formation lap, making the officials, not the driver, the cause.

Tsunoda went on to finish P10, picking up a point on his second weekend deputising for Liam Lawson at the Faenza-based squad. Audi driver Gabriel Bortoleto finished P11, just missing out on the final points-paying position.

Audi, however, does not view the situation in the same way, and will now have 96 hours in which to lodge an actual appeal of the stewards' verdict.

Audi has issued a statement, saying: "Following the Italian Grand Prix, we raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4, which requires a driver who causes an extra formation lap to enter the pit lane and resume the race from there.

"The Stewards issued a decision of No Further Action, and we have notified our intention to appeal. As the matter is now subject to the FIA appeal process, we will not comment further at this stage."

title: Liam Lawson details cause of Red Bull frustration: 'I didn't mean to'
excerpt:
Liam Lawson detailed the cause of a frustrating Italian Grand Prix for the Red Bull driver, revealing an incident with Nico Hulkenberg that he "didn't mean" to happen.

The New Zealander started from the pit lane following a rear-wing change but made contact with Hulkenberg early in the race.

He had made good ground prior to the red flag, with the incident with Hulkenberg occurring after the race restarted.

It broke Lawson's front wing, which forced him to the back by some distance, ground he could not make up due to everyone changing tyres during the red-flag stoppage.

Lawson had to settle for 14th in the end, with him pinning the clash with the Audi driver as the reason for a bad result.

Discussing his race, Lawson told select media, including RacingNews365: "Yep, I had a good first lap from the pit lane and made up quite a few places.

"Then, at the restart, I lost part of my front wing with Nico. So yeah, I had to box for a new one and lost like 30 seconds.

"So it's a shame we had very good speed in the race, but with the way the strategy was, obviously nobody really boxed after that, other than the guys that boxed under the VSC. So we just had too much time to make up."

Lawson's apology

It was not just at the first corner following the restart that an incident happened between the pair, as another clash unfolded at Turn 4.

Lawson, unsure exactly what happened, pinned it on him doing exactly what Hulkenberg had done to him at the first corner, but conceded that he did not mean to make contact.

Asked what happened with Hulkenberg, Lawson began explaining: "I was next to him, and he just kept coming over at the entry to Turn 1.

"I wasn't trying to..." The media then interjected and asked about Turn 4. An initially confused Lawson replied: "Probably exactly what he did to me. I probably did it to him. I lost my mirror, so I couldn't see on the right-hand side of my car.

"But if I squeezed him, which maybe I did, I didn't mean to. But maybe, obviously, he didn't mean to do it to me either. But it broke my front wing, and that's not what you want."

title: Yuki Tsunoda learns fate after Italian GP stewards' investigation
excerpt:
Yuki Tsunoda has held onto his point-scoring result at the Italian Grand Prix.

The Japanese driver's substitute duties at Racing Bulls continued at Monza as he continues to stand in for Liam Lawson, who is driving Isack Hadjar's Red Bull car.

After enduring a difficult qualifying session on Saturday, Tsunoda progressed during the race and crossed the line in 10th place.

However, an investigation was looming over his head due to a starting infringement, which occurred when he appeared to have an issue on the grid before the lights went out.

Tsunoda was pointing at an unusual angle, having moved into his grid slot late after realising he was originally pulling into the wrong box.

After deliberating the matter, the stewards found that Tsunoda's actions did not completely cause an aborted start, resulting in no further action being taken.

Below, you can see the stewards' full explanation of their verdict.

The Race Director, in evidence, stated that it was his call, based on the behaviour of the car on the approach to the grid box, to commence an extra formation lap. He stated he was not comfortable starting the race with the car in that position.

The team representative stated that:

(i) The car was not in a “false start” position – referring to Article B5.1.1c of the F1 regulations, because no contact patch of the front tyres was outside the grid box lines (front and side)

(ii) At the Drivers meeting, the Race Director advised that for the start, the track limits were the pit walls and in this case, even though the car was pointed to the right, it had at least 4 metres of space to move off from the start

(iii) No other driver was impacted by the position of Car 22

(iv) The driver of Car 22 was not the “cause” of the extra formation lap.

(v) At no time was the team advised that Race Control considered Car 22 to be the cause of the extra formation lap. The Stewards agree with the points above and consider that the extra formation lap resulted from the Race Director’s assessment of the situation, rather than being directly caused by the driver of Car 22.

Further, Article B5.9.4 goes on to specify that if a driver who causes the extra formation lap and is then able to start the extra formation lap, he must enter the Pit Lane at the end of the lap and start from the Pit Lane. It is only then, if the driver fails to do this, that the mandatory penalty of a Stop and Go penalty is imposed. In other words, the penalty is for failing to come into the Pit Lane and start from there. The penalty is not for causing the extra formation lap, if indeed, he caused the extra formation lap in the first place.

A critical issue emerges here, in that in order to comply with the requirement to enter and start from the Pit Lane, a driver would need to know that he was the cause of the extra formation lap. The team representative quoted situations where extra formation laps have been commenced due to extraneous circumstances such as the position of a photographer etc. In this case, no message was sent to the team or the driver, advising them that they were the cause of the extra formation lap.

The team, based on the fact that the car was positioned within its starting grid box in compliance with the regulations, had, in our determination, no reason to instruct its driver to enter and start from the Pit Lane.

Accordingly, irrespective of whether or not the driver directly caused the extra formation lap, the team and driver were unaware that they were being considered as the cause, therefore we determine that we are unable to impose a Stop and Go penalty in this case, and decide to take no further action.

We note that the Race Director acted in good faith and out of an abundance of caution in ordering an extra formation lap. We further note that the FIA might wish to consider implementing a process to advise teams and drivers if they are considered to be the cause of an extra formation lap, so that they are then able to comply with the requirements of Article B5.9.4.

title: Lewis Hamilton calls for major Ferrari change: 'There are no rules'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has called on Ferrari to introduce rules of engagement after his incident with Charles Leclerc on the opening lap of the Italian Grand Prix.

The Monegasque driver took the start from third on the grid, with Hamilton positioned behind him as the team went in the hunt for a home victory.

However, Hamilton was pushed wide by Leclerc as they went side-by-side through the first corner and skated through the gravel, dropping down into the midpack.

Hamilton voiced his frustration over team radio at the time, and insisted after the race that the team must come up with ground rules going forward.

“I think it comes down to rules of engagement,” Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

“When I was at Mercedes, we had written rules of engagement.

“We never really, really had it too bad. There was a moment between me and Nico [Rosberg] a couple of times, but more often not, it was good.

“Here, there are no rules. We need to address that.”

Ferrari's race went from bad to worse just moments later after Leclerc crashed into the barrier at the final corner, forcing race control to deploy a red flag.

Hamilton was then forced into a recovery drive as the front-runners streaked away, and he believes the red flag further dented his chances as he felt the medium tyre that he switched to was the wrong choice.

“It [the Turn 1 incident] was very bad for the team, and obviously it put us way back in positions,” he said.

“I just tried to reset, and I was like, 'okay, I'll try and catch up, and then obviously we had to stop.

“I think I put the wrong tyres on, probably.”

title: Lando Norris issues 'fair' u-turn after Oscar Piastri radio frustration
excerpt:
Lando Norris has denied that Oscar Piastri's driving was out of line towards the end of the Italian Grand Prix.

The duo were involved in a late-race scrap for fourth place as McLaren looked to bring home a solid points haul after back-to-back victories at the last two rounds.

However, the race almost ended in disaster as, in the closing laps of the race, Norris attacked Piastri into Turn 4.

The reigning champion was forced to skate over the grass before settling back in behind his team-mate, expressing over team radio that he was pushed wide.

But Norris changed his tone after climbing out of the car, telling media including RacingNews365: “No, it was okay.

“I just need to review things, but it's just the perception of when you're in the car, when someone's opening the gap a bit and then goes straight.

“You get that perception when you're going at 200 miles per hour. So that's all.

“I think what he did was fair.”

Norris ended the race ahead of Piastri after moving in front of the Australian on the final lap with a move on the approach to the Ascari chicane.

Despite his team radio anger at the time, Norris insists he enjoyed the battle.

“It's just when you're in the moment, and you're half on the grass, you don't realise how quickly things can end pretty badly,” he said.

“Just in the heat of the moment, but no from that side, it was fine and it was a good battle. A good result from a tough race.”
